eligibility_reason: A pre-registered, high-powered registered report (N = 1,459 MTurk US workers, new data) whose classic-ISE conditions follow Thürmer & McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) 'very closely' and whose pure-bystander conditions re-test the bystander ISE of Sutton et al. (2006); the authors frame it as 'confirming its replicability' and state their classic-ISE results 'mirror those of existing research (Thürmer & McCrea, 2018, Experiment 3)'. The paper also has new theory-testing aims (behavioural bystander ISE), which get no entry.

effects.original_title: Beyond motivated reasoning: Hostile reactions to critical comments from the outgroup
effects.original_authors: Thürmer, J. Lukas; McCrea, Sean M.
effects.outcome: Bonus (0-12 cents) awarded to the commenter, costly to the participant (behavioural ISE)
effects.contrast: Criticism of the ingroup (Americans) from an ingroup (US) source vs an outgroup (Singapore) source (Contrast 1)
effects.description: Experiment 3 of Thürmer & McCrea (2018) found that US participants withheld more of a costly bonus from a commenter criticizing Americans when the commenter was from Singapore (outgroup) than when from the US (ingroup), i.e. a behavioural intergroup sensitivity effect.
effects.citation_sentence: To ensure a stringent test of our hypotheses, we followed the procedures by Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) very closely. We used the same established manipulation for the classic ISE, self-report measures that are used widely in ISE research (Hornsey & Imani, 2004), and the same behavioural measure.
effects.evidence: Results 4.3.1 (p. 6-7): 'In line with our prediction, Contrast 1 was significant, t(1,455) = -4.503, p < .001, r = .117, indicating a behavioural classic ISE.' Limitations (p. 10): 'the classic ISE paradigm (i.e., the US and Singapore conditions) was adapted from and results mirror those of existing research (Thürmer & McCrea, 2018, Experiment 3). Specifically, US-American participants were willing to punish a commenter from Singapore criticizing their group.' Table 5: bonus 8.285 vs 7.097, d = 0.342.
effects.notes: Self-replication (same authors). Replication type: authors followed the procedure 'very closely' with the same manipulation, same behavioural measure, same population (CloudResearch MTurk US); deliberate changes were adding the bystander cells, moving constructiveness before threat, and adding an identification measure after the behavioural DV — close experiment is a plausible alternative; codebook tiebreaker (direct vs close -> direct) applied. The paper never uses the word 'replication' for this test but frames the RR as confirming the ISE's replicability. Exploratory Johnson-Neyman analyses show the classic behavioural ISE only at identification >= 2.45 ('in line with' Thürmer et al., 2019), but the registered contrast is significant overall and the authors 'establish the ISE as an empirical fact'. Author first names taken from this paper's byline (same authors); reference list gives only initials.

effects.original_title: Beyond motivated reasoning: Hostile reactions to critical comments from the outgroup
effects.original_authors: Thürmer, J. Lukas; McCrea, Sean M.
effects.outcome: Self-reported message motive (constructiveness) and message threat ratings of the critical comment
effects.contrast: Criticism of the ingroup (Americans) from an ingroup (US) source vs an outgroup (Singapore) source (Contrast 1)
effects.description: The classic intergroup sensitivity effect in self-reports: criticism of one's group is judged less constructive and more threatening when it comes from an outgroup member than from an ingroup member (reported in Thürmer & McCrea, 2018, with measures adapted from Hornsey & Imani, 2004).
effects.citation_sentence: To ensure a stringent test of our hypotheses, we followed the procedures by Thürmer and McCrea (2018, Experiment 3) very closely. We used the same established manipulation for the classic ISE, self-report measures that are used widely in ISE research (Hornsey & Imani, 2004), and the same behavioural measure.
effects.evidence: Results 4.3.1 (p. 7): 'Parallel analyses of the self-report measures showed that Contrast 1 was significant for message motive, t(1,455) = -15.104, p < .001, r = .369, and for message threat, t(1,455) = 7.081, p < .001, r = .183. Consistent with the classic ISE (e.g., Hornsey & Imani, 2004) participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by outgroup criticism than ingroup criticism.' Discussion: 'Registered analyses revealed strong evidence for the classic ISE across behavioural and self-report measures'.
effects.notes: Unit-of-coding judgment: the paper treats the self-report ISE and the behavioural (costly) ISE as theoretically distinct findings (separate hypotheses: norms vs identity), so they are coded as two claims; a second coder could merge this row with s1:classic_ise_behavioural (same original, same result). Original attribution is ambiguous: the self-report items are 'directly adapted from Hornsey and Imani (2004)' and the results cite Hornsey & Imani (2004, https://doi.org/10.1177/0146167203261295) as the exemplar, while the simulation section reports self-report ISE effects 'between d = 0.630 and d = 1.005 in Thürmer & McCrea, 2018', so the immediate original whose procedure was followed is Thürmer & McCrea (2018, Exp. 3). If attributed to Hornsey & Imani (2004) (Australian participants, different groups), type would be close extension. Measure order changed (motive before threat) — close experiment also plausible.

effects.original_title: Reactions to internal and external criticism of outgroups: Social convention in the intergroup sensitivity effect
effects.original_authors: Sutton, R.; Elder, T.; Douglas, K.
effects.outcome: Self-reported message motive (constructiveness) and message threat ratings of criticism directed at an uninvolved outgroup
effects.contrast: Criticism of an outgroup (South Africans) from a same-group (South African) source vs a different-outgroup (Singapore) source (Contrast 2, pure bystander ISE)
effects.description: Uninvolved bystanders (members of a third group) also show the intergroup sensitivity effect, judging criticism of a group more negatively when it comes from an outsider than from a member of the criticized group.
effects.citation_sentence: In line with this general norm explanation, Sutton et al. (2006) observed the ISE even among uninvolved bystanders who were members of a third group (bystander ISE). ... For the bystander ISE, the involvement of the ingroup can vary: Sutton et al. (2006) compared criticism between two outgroups (in our terminology Outgroup A and Outgroup B), where the ingroup is neither the target nor the source of criticism. We thus term the resulting effect the pure bystander effect.
effects.evidence: Results 4.3.2 (p. 7): 'As predicted, a bystander ISE (Contrast 2) emerged for the self-report measures of message motive, t(1,455) = -20.208, p < .001, r = .469, and message threat, t(1,455) = 13.341, p < .001, r = .331. Consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006), participants ascribed less constructive motives to and were more threatened by between-group criticism than within-group criticism.' Discussion: 'we also found unequivocal support for the bystander ISE in self-reports.'
effects.notes: Ambiguity concerns eligibility/type more than result: the bystander test is framed as a theory test of the norm account and not called a replication, but it re-tests Sutton et al.'s (2006) pure-bystander finding with new data and the authors call the result 'consistent with the bystander ISE (e.g., Sutton et al., 2006)'. Type: the groups (US participants judging South Africa vs Singapore) and the Thürmer & McCrea comment/measures differ from Sutton et al.'s materials, so close extension (conceptual is a possible alternative). Author first names not given in the paper (reference list gives initials). NOT coded: (a) the behavioural bystander ISE — no prior published claim (the authors predicted its absence; it emerged); (b) Comparison I vs Sutton et al. (2008, book chapter) 'both effects being of similar magnitude' — exploratory here, found bystander ISE larger; (c) exploratory moderation by identification 'in line with' Thürmer et al. (2019) — different behavioural paradigm, reviewer-requested interactions non-significant; (d) serial mediation that 'confirmed past theorizing' (Hornsey & Imani, 2004; Thürmer & McCrea, 2018) — process analysis, not a separate registered test; (e) Target (Contrast 4) and Source (Contrast 3) — new exploratory contrasts.
